body:
We can invoke MSBuild to evaluate `$(OutputPath)` and we do that in the new dotnet module, because I want C# projects to be more flexible. Users could define their own output path or enable [artifacts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/sdk/artifacts-output).

However, changing the output path for existing projects is a bit delicate because the moment the projects update to the new SDK (which happens when you open a project with a new Godot version), the path changes and Godot won't be able to find the previously built DLLs. This means the inspector will be outdated until you rebuild the project, and your scenes/resources may lose data if you save them before building the project[^1].

Because of this, we'd want to keep the current output path as the default. However, I don't think we can allow changing the output path, we set it in `Sdk.props` which is evaluated very early so it propagates to subsequent MSBuild tasks and targets.

Also, to better understand your scenario. Can you explain when you use the `RuntimeIdentifier` property and for what purpose? What kind of issues are you running into? For example, I imagine the inspector is using an outdated build from before you set the `RuntimeIdentifier` property. But exporting should work, since the command we use specifies a custom output path.

[^1]: This problem already exists in some scenarios: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/90755. But changing the path would make it worse.

I am setting `RuntimeIdentifier` because I am taking a package dependency on a NuGet package with RID-specific (native) bits.  To import the package the build system requires that you specify one or more RIDs in `RuntimeIdentifier(s)` that match those RID exported by the NuGet.  In this case the RID I'm interested in is `win-x64` which is the Export RID for Godot anyway, so no problem.  Except... when you add `RuntimeIdentifier` to a csproj normally NetSDK adds the RID to the output path.  So, by default instead of `bin\Debug\net8.0` you get `bin\Debug\net8.0\win-x64`.

This is all fine.  And, as you said, this doesn't affect exporting, which works fine.  But, the editor doesn't work at all after this change.  

The `Sdk.props` does set both `BaseOutputPath` and `OutputPath`, but I suspect that the setting of `OutputPath` really has no effect because that value is recomputed by the Build target.  The Build target recomputes it as `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)\$(TargetFramework)\`.  However, there is an extensibility property `AppendTargetFrameworkToOutputPath` which controls whether `$(TargetFramework)` is actually appended.  This is **also** set to `false` by `Sdk.props` which causes the recomputation of `OutputPath` to be equal to `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)\` instead, which happens to be exactly what `Sdk.props` set it to in the first place.  So, it appears like the setting of `OutputPath` actually did something (even if it didn't).

It turns out that the real recomputation for `OutputPath` is even longer.  It is actually `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)\$(TargetFramework)\$(RuntimeIdentifier)` BUT, if `RuntimeIdentifier` is empty this becomes `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)\$(TargetFramework)\\` which is effectively the same as `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)\$(TargetFramework)\` (at least to `msbuild`).  When `RuntimeIdentifier` is NOT empty, however, then setting `AppendTargetFrameworkToOutputPath` (as `Sdk.props` does) causes the recomputation to become `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)\$(RuntimeIdentifier)`.  When `Sdk.props` sets `BaseOutputPath` to `.godot\mono\temp\bin\` this leads to a value of `.godot\mono\temp\bin\win-x64`.  Everything in `msbuild`-land **still** builds fine here, but the binaries are binplaced to `.godot\mono\temp\bin\win-x64`.

But, as far as I can tell, the Editor NEVER looks in that directory.  I'm _guessing_ it is hardcoded to look in `.godot\mono\temp\bin\`, is that true?  I tried restarting, rebuilding, cleaning, etc. everything... but could find no way to get the Editor to look in `.godot\mono\temp\bin\win-x64`.  

As a hack, I also set `AppendRuntimeIdentifierToOutputPath` to `false` which, as with `AppendTargetFrameworkToOutputPath` causes the recomputation to become `$(BaseOutputPath)\$(Configuration)` once again, and then the Editor _is_ happy.  _Hence, the suggested fix above._

**But**... it feels _ugly and brittle_.  It would be _nicer_ if the Editor just did the right thing.  If it detected the default output path that NetSDK comes up with (whatever it happens to be) and just uses it.  If the output path changes (say because `RuntimeIdentifier` is set, or `TargetPlatform` is changed) then the Editor just rebuilds everything.  That is what the normal `msbuild` workflow would do.  I'm not asking for it to work while the Editor is running, but on a clean rebuild/reopen maybe it should work?

Thank so much you for the detailed explanation.

> But, as far as I can tell, the Editor NEVER looks in that directory. I'm _guessing_ it is hardcoded to look in `.godot\mono\temp\bin\`, is that true?

Yes, right here:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/987832be460f82206fcac1467e58efbd111c5241/modules/mono/godotsharp_dirs.cpp#L141-L142

Sorry if my previous comment was confusing, when I said the new dotnet module is using MSBuild to evaluate `$(OutputPath)` I was referring to an unreleased product. The current module is still using a hardcoded path.

> If the output path changes (say because `RuntimeIdentifier` is set, or `TargetPlatform` is changed) then the Editor just rebuilds everything.

This would require implementing this proposal:

- https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2920

And keep in mind a lot of users would still prefer to keep that disabled.

> The `Sdk.props` does set both `BaseOutputPath` and `OutputPath`, but I suspect that the setting of `OutputPath` really has no effect because that value is recomputed by the Build target.

I think this is what you are referring to:

https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/3c21adb924c3c33682255711fd42a714210d8075/src/Tasks/Microsoft.NET.Build.Tasks/targets/Microsoft.NET.RuntimeIdentifierInference.targets#L338-L355

```xml
<OutputPath Condition="'$(UseArtifactsOutput)' != 'true'">$(OutputPath)$(RuntimeIdentifier)\</OutputPath>
```

It looks like it just appends to our `OutputPath` value. But it may be true that we don't need to specifically set the `OutputPath` property.

The Build target basically expects to "cons-up" the `OutputPath`.  This has been made complicated by the distributed nature of the append actions and the introduction of the "artifacts" feature.  But you can see where `OutputPath` would normally get set here:

https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/3c21adb924c3c33682255711fd42a714210d8075/src/Tasks/Microsoft.NET.Build.Tasks/targets/Microsoft.NET.DefaultOutputPaths.targets#L99C5-L99C130

```xml
<OutputPath Condition="'$(OutputPath)' == ''">$(BaseOutputPath)$(_PlatformToAppendToOutputPath)$(Configuration)\</OutputPath>
```

Then subsequent rules just append stuff to the end.  The logic in NetSDK doesn't really keep track of whether you manually set `OutputPath` after the line above.  (Maybe it should?  Seems like a bug.)  But then it just appends segments.  The `TargetPlatform` and `RuntimeIdentifier` get so appended at later points in the evaluation (oblivious to the fact that `OutputPath` didn't actually get set by the above because it was manually overridden).

My understanding is that the overall goal here is to allow multi-platform targeting out of the same enlistment.  I.e. you can build both win-x64, linux-x64, and android all from the same directory tree without the outputs conflicting (by having to write on top of each other).  You can build all platforms at the same time with the same msbuild execution.  This requires, however, that all outputs that might conflict be destined to land in different directories.  I think this makes for a much more efficient build system and works well with automation and publishing.  Given that Godot really wants to support multi-targeting for projects it would be great if it played well in this world.  If Godot could dock to the existing conventions used/enforced by NetSDK then it is much less likely to run into friction in the future.  (e.g. There really shouldn't be the need for ExportDebug or ExportRelease configurations as these concepts are already manifested by the NetSDK complex nonsense around platform\rid\publish conventions.)

---

As to keeping the code/data loaded in the Editor in sync with the code/data on disk... This problem seems bigger and has more widespread implications.  I would have to think more about this problem to have anything actually intelligent to say.  My first impressions are that this isn't really about automatically recompiling the code.  It's really a serialization synchronization problem that requires code and data to evolve along the same linear ordering.

> [!WARNING]  
> Random musing follows...

At first blush there are at least four parties that need to stay in sync:

1. The data serialization on disk (e.g. a tscn file that encodes the values of Exports).
2. The C# source on disk.
3. The data serialization active in memory in the Editor.
4. The assembly bits loaded into the Editor.

Let's assume a serialization regime with partial materialization (i.e. unknown properties are ignored during materialization) and partial materialization does NOT support round-tripping unknown data (i.e. non-materialized data is lost during reserialization).  This means that (1) can be downlevel from (2), but as soon as (2) round-trips (1) it will write it back as (1`) at the _current version_ of (2).  If (1) is uplevel from (2) then new additive data will be misinterpreted as downlevel data that was dropped during evolution.  A version of (2) _older_ than (1) should therefore NEVER be run on (1).

This is generally a pretty stable environment as long as (1) and (2) moved forward in lockstep.  (1) and (2) represent the persistent state of the system.  (2) will be used to materialize (1).  (1) and (2) can change _together_ like when source control does a sync, but this doesn't break the lockstep property.  

The same is mostly true for (3) and (4) as well.

The tricky part is when (1) and (2) both have changed, and the Editor detects it.  By the above logic it is "unsafe" to reload (3) without first reloading (4), because doing so would lead to a downlevel materialization of uplevel data.  Instead, the Editor should refuse to reload (3) until it can reload (4).  That doesn't mean it has to force a build of (2) to produce (4).  But it does mean that it shouldn't try to load (3) and display it.  Maybe it should _freeze_ the scene editor window and warn the user that a recompilation is necessary to unfreeze.  The user can then hit Build or switch back to the IDE for more editing.  This is particularly import if the Build is going to fail (due to a code bug).

The key issue is detecting that (1) is uplevel with respect to (4).  The relationship between (1) and (4) needs to be present within (1) and (3).  As a straw man, what if we consider the case where (1) includes a hash of the source (2) that produce the version of (4) that wrote (1).  If the hash of (2) that produced (1) doesn't match the hash of (2) that produced (4) then (3) should be _frozen_ until (2) is recompiled.  I'm not sure exactly what "hash (2)" should really mean but we can think on that separately.

At any rate.  If the relationship between the (4) and (2) was about linear ordering instead, then it doesn't matter what folder (4) lives in.  When it is time to recompile then just do a build to produce a new (4).  Then load that new (4) in its entirety.  Then reload (3) from (1).  All is good.
